utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krsman. Before returning to the subject we were discussing before the adjournment on Friday I'd like to return briefly to a couple of other matters. First I'd like to direct your attention to tab 13, I don't know if you have the bundle -- apparently you don't have the bundle in front of you just yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 13 contains P826, tab 7, and that's a document bearing various entries chronological entries relevant to Rajlovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to orient you quickly, Mr. Krsman, if you'll turn to the third page you'll see an entry for February 23rd, 1992, for example, which reflects assembly of Rajlovac Serb municipality and as you indicated during the course of your testimony that was the date of its establishment.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I could also -- if I could ask you to turn to an earlier entry of February 12th, 1992, which appears about three entries before that one, and it begins Lemez land surveyor. It mentions a meeting on Sunday in Reljevo and it makes reference to drawing the map of the new municipality borders. And then it continues with some demographic indications referring to the local area of Zuc Dolac. And the entries that I see are in two columns, so next to the entry for Serbs it says, 368 and 1470, next to the entry for Muslims, 85 and 346, for Croats 7 and 26 and for Romanies, 11 and 96. So first of all, Mr. Krsman, I'm wondering if you can explain to the Court what the two entries specifically reflect, that is the two entries for each of the listed ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I'm seeing this for the first time. I didn't write this so I really don't know what all this means. I can only assume that as it says, Romanies, 11, that they lived up there by the refuse dump. I know that there were Croats. As to the rest, I really can't say. It's probably a percentage of some kind, the number of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well to the best of your recollection, at or in February of 1992, would that be a roughly accurate reflection of the number of inhabitants in the local area of Zuc Dolac, that is Serbs, 1470, Muslims 346, Croats 26, and Romanies, 96?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't guarantee that that is it because I really don't know about these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I appreciate that I'm asking you about very specific figures. More generally, however, I'd like to know if that approximates generally your understanding of the approximate population figures of that area in February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my knowledge goes with respect to the Zuc Dolac municipality, all I can say is that I knew the people that I associated with, even with the population census it wasn't my region, it wasn't the area where I conducted a population census so I really can't say whether this corresponds to the situation on the ground. I assume that the person who wrote this would give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And ask -- again, I'm not trying to push you for information you don't have, just trying to ask questions that may elicit such information as you do have. So irrespective of your precise knowledge of the exact population figures, were you aware in February of 1992 that in Zuc Dolac there was a preponderance of Serbs and then the -- and then some hundreds of Muslims followed by a relative handful of Croats and Romanies?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking that would be the percentage but I don't know what this means, 1470 Serbs, there certainly weren't that many Serbs there. Perhaps the figure of 368 is the correct figure. I don't know what this 1470 refers to because I'm quite sure there weren't that many Serbs in Zuc Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I asked about your understanding of the general proportion of Serbs and Muslims and Croats because we had addressed that issue in your earlier testimony in looking at the composition of the newly established Rajlovac municipality in February of 1992. And for your benefit I'll just note that the populated areas that comprised the Rajlovac municipality are found at tab 12, listed in the law on the establishment of Rajlovac municipality. And we talked about the composition of Rajlovac a couple of times and on Friday, I had again asked you about that in connection with the law I just referred to at tab 12, and you mentioned -- I directed your attention to Ahatovici and then I asked you about which of the other populated areas were populated with Muslims. You mentioned -- I asked you about Brijesce and then you mentioned Smiljevici, Brijesce and the 21st of May and said the rest were all ethnically pure areas. So I take it that would be correct, that it's not accurate to say that the rest were all ethnically pure areas but at least Dolac and Zuc were populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I'll be very precise in my answer, Zuc was an ethnically pure Serb village whereas Dolac is a continuation of that village just like Smiljevici is a continuation of Zabrdje village. And in Dolac you had Romanies, Croats, and Muslims living there. The Roma are a people who do not have a permanent place of residence. They lived up there because there was a refuse depot there. That's why they lived there. They made their livelihood on the basis of that depot and I know that Zuc is purely Serb, but Dolac, I do allow for the possibility that there was populated by the Muslims, Roma and so on. So the first number, 368 would be correct, 85 Muslims would be correct, 7 Croats, and 11 Roma. Now, all the others expelled all the Serbs from Zuc on the 17th of May. The Muslims did. When the genocide took place and the expulsion from Pogaric [phoen], and not a single Serb was left living in Zuc after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By what date were there no longer any Muslims living in the Rajlovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Rajlovac there were Muslims throughout the war but a very small number. And I think sometime after August, that there were not large numbers of Muslims as there were prior to the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, on Friday, we also had the opportunity to look briefly at what in fact I think Mr. Josse asked you some questions about the extent of and form of military preparation by Serbs in the Rajlovac area. And if I understood you correctly, you were saying that -- you spoke about the surprise experienced by the Serbs of Rajlovac on -- upon May 8th and the fact that not a single trench was dug or any "any military formations of that kind." And that was at page 26 of the LiveNote. So did I understand that correctly, Mr. Krsman, that you were -- you wanted the Court to understand that the Serbs of Rajlovac had no military formations of any kind before May 8th, which was the date that you described an attack on the Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the first part of your question, my answer to that is that we really did not have a single solitary trench dug out, not a single trench. Now as far as military formations were concerned, we were organised as I've already said as village watches and we were organised to put up a defence at the separation line towards Sokolje, according to the areas we lived in and according to the number of houses in the area, until the army of Republika Srpska was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it may be a problem of translation and semantics but village watch to me connotes a kind of very informal neighbourhood, extremely loosely organised group, in contrast to something organised like a company under the command of the army or the TO or the police. So -- so is it correct that you're making a distinction between those two kinds of groups and indicating that prior to May 8th only the former, very loosely associated group existed?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I've already said that, that we had agreement with our neighbours the Muslims, that we had mined the area the terrain and we just had these groups that reconnoitered and observed and were prepared to sound the alarm more than anything else, rather than to defend ourselves in organised fashion, which showed -- which -- and this is what happened when we had to move back into the depth of our territory for one kilometre when the attack was launched on May the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn your attention next, then, to tab 21, please? And that's P372, Your Honour. Now, P372, Mr. Krsman, is an order from the Rajlovac municipality Crisis Staff in April 1992 that directs the following: The active observation of the entire territory of Rajlovac municipality is being ordered, and platoon commanders and the Crisis Staff are to be informed on everything noticed. Number 2, TO unit members are forbidden to drink alcohol while on duty. The work of catering facilities after 2200 hours is also forbidden. Number 3, directs one policeman and two TO members to be at the checkpoint towards the distribution centre 24 hours a day. And orders that the Rajlovac platoon commander and the commander of the illegible unit are placed in charge in cooperation with the police commander and finally indicates that all other activities are to be done in accordance with the previously determined obligations on all territories. Mr. Krsman, what is the Rajlovac -- who was the Rajlovac platoon commander, first of all?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a broad question. The commander of the Rajlovac platoon -- well, there wasn't one commander so I don't know what you have in mind. In my company, I had three platoon commanders. So that's one -- just one part of the unit. Furthermore it says here the distribution centre and the checkpoint there, that isn't my area of responsibility so I don't know which Crisis Staff this is and what this refers to. We had a number of Crisis Staff, Zabrdje, Rajlovac, the Crisis Staff of, I don't know, Dobrosevici probably. I don't know who signed this. I can't see a signature. All I can see is that the date is the 9th of April which is already the time when the fires had flared up throughout Bosnia and Bozic [phoen] petrol pump. This might be the Rajlovac Crisis Staff together with the Rajlovac municipality. And as you can see, the police was still operating so this is in cooperation with the police chief. We didn't have a police station in Zabrdje. It was in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say, then, that at least as of April 9th, defensive activities undertaken to protect against various risks, were undertaken by both the police of Rajlovac and the Rajlovac platoon or platoons?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this sort of observation was set up. There is nothing that I challenge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was it the Rajlovac platoon that received the 202 weapons that came from the Rajlovac barracks? Or was it some other formation?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, a platoon is -- has a maximum much 30 men and I said that our village, Zabrdje, received 202 pieces of ammunition -- pieces of weapons which means that all the able bodied men from my village, I don't know what this platoon is, what platoon this is, what it refers to, perhaps it's a police platoon. Well, it says here the commander of the Reljevo unit and that's a village which is opposite in Bosnia, which was organised in some other way apart from the platoons and that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was a Serb village also, I think you indicated to us the other day, correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So apart from the police, in the Rajlovac municipality, which presumably operated in the various populated areas you described in your earlier testimony, how many organised platoons were operating in the Rajlovac municipality? Either in Reljevo, Zabrdje or any of the other populated areas that comprised Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Zabrdje. As to the other places, I really don't know. I wasn't interested. Most probably they were organised according to the number of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And their activities were being at least coordinated, as this order indicates, and as the anniversary speech that we looked at the other day also indicated, by the Crisis Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't coordinated until the army of Republika Srpska was established. We all had our own problems and they were all different problems, not of the same nature. And if Reljevo was two or three kilometres away from Zabrdje, the people over there thought that the war would be in Slovenia or somewhere far away at the beginning. So you must realise that we Serbs really did not believe that a war would break out but with that first attack on the 8th of May, everything slowly began to change and the Territorial Defence began to be established as was the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- I don't want to dwell on this for too long but I think it's important to separate what you claim to be the subjective impression of the Serbian population about the likelihood of war from the activities that were undertaken prior to the war. Now, you say there was no -- they weren't coordinated until the army of Republika Srpska was established. I don't want to compare the level of coordination and the any improvement in coordination that might have taken place after the establishment of the RS, but this order directs the active observation of the entire territory of Rajlovac municipality, and states that platoon commanders and the Crisis Staff are to be informed on everything noticed. So isn't it correct to say that by April 9th, 1992, that effort was being undertaken by the Crisis Staff over the breadth of the Rajlovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I can say. Take a look at this order. It should say at the end who it is addressed to, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. It doesn't say who it's addressed to. So nothing was formally or officially established. This is something written out on a white piece of paper says Crisis Staff, but if it doesn't say who the addressees are, perhaps this order never reached anyone. Perhaps it was sent to one person or one addressee or more, we don't know. And as the war progressed, we organised ourselves to protect our lives and our property. So that's all I can say. I really don't know what else to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, and this is I think the last question I'll ask about this order, you don't really want this Court to believe that this order was written out and then directed to some fictitious and invented TO units or some non-existent and fanciful platoons?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. Certainly not. It was certainly sent to the police station and perhaps a platoon but I don't know which platoon. It wasn't the platoon from Zabrdje at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I indicated that we would return to the area we had been discussing when we adjourned on Friday, and if I recall correctly at that time, we had addressed the remarks of Mr. Trifko Radic at the January 1993 Bosnian Serb Assembly about the evil that we, meaning the Serbs, as Mr. Radic was speaking, had caused them, presumably meaning the Muslims and Croats. And I had asked you about your knowledge of shelling, and that is massive shelling of areas heavily populated by civilians in Sarajevo, and you had indicated that -- let me be precise about that, if I may. You were unaware of any targeting of civilian areas or civilians. You recall that general discussion, Mr. Krsman?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in connection with that, then, I'd like to play an intercepted telephone conversation that took place on the 11th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's found at tab 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Needs a number, as far as I can see, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1134, Your Honour, B/C/S transcript P1134.A, and the English transcript P1134.A.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is relatively long. I took a look at it to see if it was amenable to clipping. I didn't conclude that at the end it would be helpful to the Court to do so. So I would like to play that in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Smajic: Can we have Colonel Kobagovic [as interpreted]. Let me give you two sentences so we can continue talking. If you've heard of my name. Then, okay. I completed military academy in Belgrade. I was an active officer for 7 and a half years, and I was a journalist for 14 and -- or 15 years. Gagovic: So now you have a very nice job. Smajic: Well, it all depends on how you decide to treat it. Colonel, kindly listen to me for a couple of minutes and it may be useful -- it may be mutually useful and mutually beneficial. I'm a local of Brijesce near the school. I have a couple [as interpreted] of friends and I have relatives, and I have relatives in the Rajlovac barracks, both officers and civilians. Yesterday, all day, I did not work at Yutel. I have not worked in Yutel for four days now and I have reasons why I don't work. After the tragic event two days ago, we inspected the villages of Sokolje, this mosque, we were in Zabrdje. Mirko Krajisnik expressed his condolences, we returned by the people with a good reason and yesterday I was for the first time in the Rajlovac barracks. We inspected the barracks. We calmed people down. We saw what people were doing and we asked them not to provoke anybody, to be dignified and that the army should withdraw in a dignified way without the involvement of politics, and it was calm yesterday. I was at -- the television interrupted me at the time and what happened yesterday, an hour ago, guided missiles, I told you that I completed a military academy, and I know what weapons are, what weapons are. Guided missiles hit six times and struck at the building of the television. After that, five or six missiles fell over the television building. I believe that the tower was targeted. Gagovic: When you're talking about guided missiles, do you mean guided missiles? Smajic: Yes, guided missiles. Gagovic: They have a target and they can hit it. 3.000, yes, 3 kilometres. So after they missed -- Smajic: Actually, I don't know if they missed or didn't. Gagovic: Yes. Smajic: General cannon fire began including attack on the settlements, Boljakov Potok up there. What is it called? Sokolje and Brijesce Brdo, the areas we visited yesterday. We begged them and asked them and informed them about everything. Inhabitants of these hamlets went with us yesterday to the barracks and they talked to relevant officers. Miletic was out of the barracks and the officers in charge of security talked to us. Some of them are my relatives and let me tell you straight away: They saw for themselves that they wouldn't be the first ones to open the fire. However, we have evidence from the day before yesterday, we have photographs, and binocular proofs, and so on and so forth. Evidence that a provocation aimed at the barracks of Rajlovac came from the hill of Zuc. After that, enormous fire was opened at those settlements. Something else happened today. I'm now at the TV building. Bullets, shells, anti-aircraft projectiles, and who knows what else is flying over the building. In any case, salvos continue to fall down on those settlements. I assure you that it has been agreed upon the day before yesterday that nobody is allowed to fire one shot. Because they don't want and not wish to use automatic weapons of any kind or weapons before it is decided what will happen with the municipality of Rajlovac. As a human being I would like to tell you that it is 99 per cent sure that it was the case of international provocation -- intentional provocation because three settlements with inhabitants of pure Muslim nationality have been frantically shelled. As a human being I would like to warn you so that you can consider your position. Because we ought to live as human beings, as fathers, or members of families and so on. The war will be over. Therefore, I wish to inform you, the firsthand knowledge. Gagovic: Smajic. Smajic: Please. Gagovic: I respect it completely and I appreciate such information. Smajic: Yes. Okay. Gagovic: But just before 2000 hours. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: Colonel Miletic, I think you know him personally. Smajic: I do, I called him ten times. Gagovic: He called me and said, Please they are shelling us from mortars again, from the region of Boljakov Potok, and I read as he said, Bresko Brdo. Smajic: Sir. Gagovic: He swore to me. I have written here. I asked him again and repeated it. I give Miletic his phone number 450973 to Mr. Abdic. I called Mr. Abdic and I said to Mr. Fikret, from this region and to intervene, to stop it, to prevent destroying facilities, houses and especially to prevent killing people. Smajic: Sir. Gagovic: Yes. Smajic: Take my word for that. I swear by my children. First of all, you know that mortars shells can be heard at least from Boljakov Potok up to here. Only the river and one road divide us. I assure you we had meeting on that side exactly because our premises, my premises are next to Boljakovo side. And we were just beginning -- bringing our meeting to an end in a better spirit and encouraged by the decision that there would be no more shooting and that everything is fine. And after that we got up, put the chairs back, and two terrible detonations took place on the 6th floor. On the 6th floor they shook us up. We all jumped and ran out and went to the ground floor. Gagovic: I believe that. Smajic: General cannon fire started ten minutes later towards that settlement. Trust me, I'm telling you. Secondly, these people from Sokolje, Boljakovo, and Brijesce hill came yesterday and asked through us ... I informed Miletic, Abdic, and all relevant people about it. They are requesting an expertise, military and your expertise from Lukavica. From Rajlovac. UNPROFOR, EC, whoever wants to. Monitors, helicopters, reconnaissance aircrafts, everything, to identify positions from which it is allegedly being fired at the barracks in Rajlovac. Please. Today ... I received 100 calls from Sokolje, Brijesce, and so on. People have their eyes fixed upon thee because they think I can do something about it. They say that absolutely everyone is in the cellars and shelters and that it is not logical to open such heavy fire using artillery pieces at them. I want to assure that that was the case. Gagovic: I agree with you, there are so-called free riflemen. I also assure that you these units called JNA, or so-called JNA, as it is popular nowadays to call them. Smajic: Do you hear these detonations? Gagovic: I hear them. They are going in all directions. Those are light rocket-launchers. After that, up there in Faletici, after requisition of assets, people armed themselves. And they are carrying these tubes, two missiles on the back. They get caught in an ambush and fire from another place, and that is what is called free marksman. Nobody controls them and commands them. I guarantee that. "The ones who are under military command are certainly not using ... I was assuring Mr. Abdic of that a while ago and they were assuring me for two or three nights that they were firing from the barracks Marshal Tito. Today I enabled four of there man from Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina TO to enter the barracks and to see for themselves that nobody is firing from that barracks. "I told them this: If you want 40 and not only four of your monitors to check each of the JNA units, we guarantee your safety and everything else. Let them come and see for themselves that nobody is shooting from the JNA areas. Smajic: Well, who fired at the television just now? Can you give me an answer to that? Gagovic: That is, if that was a missile, as you said, it was not a guided missile. Those were light rocket-launchers, because guided missiles are antitank. Smajic: This is not a light launcher. That is a huge shell. We thought that it was an airplane flying over. Gagovic: No, no, no. That is -- you know exactly that. This is that missile. It is 128 millimetres but it is called light because it has one tube. It is a part of multiple launchers the army has. Territorial Defence had them earlier. 11 launchers of that kind disappeared when Faletici were destroyed. And those launchers are used by -- to tell you the truth, I have no idea who was using them. So that's about it. I will do whatever I can to prevent what is coming, especially the victims. Smajic: Everything is breaking apart here. Gagovic: I also asked for Hadzici. Our repair and maintenance depot has been attacked. Maybe you've been there before. Smajic: Yes, I have. I have friends up there. Gagovic: So there you go. You know what repair and maintenance depot is. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: Does that -- the army is leaving any way. That repair and maintenance depot will remain for the use of the municipality of Hadzici. Isn't that a sin and disgrace to attack it and destroy it when they know that it will be destroyed if it is taken away in such manner. Smajic: That's true. Gagovic: It doesn't make. Smajic: I understand it completely. I also wanted to ask, beg Miletic yesterday. However, he wasn't there to ... Gagovic: You have his number. If you don't have it, it's 450973. Miletic's number. Smajic: 45973? Gagovic: 450. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: 973. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: Because of me, so that you don't think that Gagovic or the units from Lukavica are shooting even though I am not. Someone else is commander. Smajic: I know. Gagovic: But I'm in charge of communications between -- I mediate between TO, and I don't know. These negotiators and units. So you could see for yourself that you could see for yourself what kind of reports should be submitted I forwarded it to operations centre because I cannot -- if commander reports so then it ... Smajic: Okay, that's clear, you see, sir. There has been shelling at those settlements for the last hour. Well, if -- the officer from Rajlovac confirmed to me that two shells were fired this evening as a provocation, as a response, general shelling took place. I mean, I cannot understand that. There were 250 houses out of 300 destroyed in Sokolje. Gagovic: I can believe that. You see ... Smajic: Is it really necessary to open such fire just because of two shells, especially if it hadn't been confirmed that they really came from the direction? Because, nowadays anybody can provoke, anybody who has weapons, you know. And from the hill of Zuc ... For example, people from Sokolje claim that the provocation came from the hill of Zuc and was directed at the barracks in order to destroy Sokolje, and that is exactly what is happening. Gagovic: I don't know. I can't exclude even such a possibility, so I don't exclude even such possibility. Smajic: Can I ask you something as a human being? Gagovic: Always. Smajic: Please, if it is possible, after an hour of salvos and destroying, stop it. I will get in touch with Miletic first thing in the morning. I will ask him as a human being since he is leaving in a few days. Gagovic: Yes, I know. Smajic: I will ask him to visit together those villages, to go down to the little river to visit Zabrdje, Sokolje, and Gornje Brijesce. So that he can see for himself that people are saying. Well, it is impossible that 1500 people are lying. Gagovic: Well, I agree ... Smajic: That is impossible, believe me. Gagovic: ... completely with you. But, you see, who is then the one who ... of all these measures and manners. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: Negotiations and talks, peaceful solutions, involving the man whom I respect very much, Fikret Abdic. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: Peace supporter, businessman. I guarantee that he's not interested in any army and war but in the economy; however, there is always somebody who disturbs, prevents, makes barricades. The last reports says ... Smajic: Extremists on both sides. Gagovic: You see, they are reporting now, I don't know, that Vrbanja bridge has been mined. There are gas bottles. I mean cistern ... a cistern is placed on this bridge. Smajic: Yes. Gagovic: There are gas cisterns on the second bridge. Does Sarajevo need it? Smajic: Colonel, I thank you for your attention and your time. Gagovic: There you go. Smajic: But I am begging you. Gagovic: Thank you. Likewise. Smajic: I'm asking you to try to intervene and to stop all those salvos and destroying. I swear to you that the last three or four days ... I gave up my work in journalism until this madness is gone ... to help, to connect. I have been mediating the whole day today, to organise a meeting between Momcilo Krajisnik from Pale and Fikret Abdic. Gagovic: I have also suggested that, to be honest with you. Smajic: I'm working on that. Gagovic: Because people don't want to understand that this party has significant influence. It has. They are armed on the large scale. They took the arms from Faletici. They have lethal weapons but they don't have influence. There isn't, there isn't ... Smajic: Thanks a lot. Gagovic: Thank you. Smajic: If you can consider, do something to stop this fire. Gagovic: Do everything I can. Smajic: Please. Gagovic: For sure, I'll do what I can. Smajic: Because nobody moved from there. The children are there. The houses are built from concrete blocks. All life is built in there. Please. Gagovic: I agree with you completely and I'll do everything I can, I assure you. Smajic: Thank you. I'll call Pale now since I have to let them know regarding Abdic. Gagovic: Cheers. Smajic: Thank you. Have a nice day. Gagovic: Thanks. You too."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just waiting to see if the French translation was fine. I might note that on page 8 I noticed a discrepancy between the English translation in print and what was reflected in the ongoing translation from the booth, and it seemed to occur at a time when someone was either turning a page or there was a lag in the translation. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were a few more, Mr. Tieger, I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krsman, you know who Milosav Gagovic was and what his position was in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Gagovic was but I do know who Zekerijah Smajic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I indicate to you that Milosav Gagovic was an assistant commander at the forward command post at Lukavica, would that jog your memory at all about him?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who he was but now that you've jogged my memory, I think I know who he is so you can ask me questions based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And you indicated you knew who Mr. Smajic was. I take it that on May 11th, 1992, Gagovic was an officer stationed at Lukavica and Smajic was, as he indicated, a journalist and I presume a Bosniak journalist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he was a Muslim journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, without going into too many of the finer details, Mr. Krsman, this intercept addresses and reflects a large-scale shelling and subsequent destruction of a good portion of Sokolje as discussed between Smajic and Gagovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as Gagovic indicated -- Gagovic at least was telling Smajic that the shelling had been done with the weapons taken from Faletici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know where Faletici is, and that was one of the central depots of the Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia. That depot was under the control of Muslims and they are the ones who took those weapons out of that depot because the depot was in the territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krsman, you know that's not entirely true because you know that the SDS took over a great number of weapons from Faletici, and in fact it's the SDS to which Gagovic is referring in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, then you're not familiar with the map or with the situation. Faletici was under Muslim control and the Territorial Defence in Faletici could be entered only by Muslims, and it was the Muslims who took all that from Faletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, when I refer to the SDS, I mean more generically either the forces of the SDS or the forces of the then political authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not a member of the SDS. I still I was in the defence of Republika Srpska from day 1 to the last day. The SDS does not equal Republika Srpska. It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you weren't a member of the SDS so I take it that's your way of saying you don't know what the SDS was doing. Would you know whether or not the forces of the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over equipment and weapons from Faletici prior to the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again, most of that equipment in Faletici was taken by Muslims, 100 per cent -- I'm 100 per cent sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not the forces of the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over weapons from Faletici before May?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The depot in Faletici is in the territory under the control of Muslims. Only one of its parts is on the other side, and is connected to the territory under the control of Serbs. I know with reliability that they even put up their guards. The Muslims did. I don't know who took the weapons but I know that the Muslims took most of the weapons in the Faletici depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it seems you're giving an answer based on logic and, if I hear you correctly, you can't tell me whether the forces of Serbian Republic took weapons or how many, is that basically it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying this only because this is mentioned in here. Otherwise I was not there. I'm not able to tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, then, to, I think, a new tab. Probably have to distribute that, Your Honour. These are the minutes of the meeting of the national Security Council on 24 April 1992. Actually the minutes of the meeting of the national Security Council and the government. That's P65, tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a number already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to the decisions that appear under item 1, and looking in particular at the 8th listed decision, which indicates as follows: "A decision was passed on making a complete register of weapons and equipment taken over from Faletici on determining the issuing and storing of part of the equipment and weapons currently not being used. Radovan Karadzic, in charge." Now, Mr. Krsman, that's a reference to the takeover of weapons and equipment from Faletici by the forces of the authorities of the Serbian Republic about which you apparently were unaware; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here the decision is to be passed to establish a full unit with the weapons that were taken over. That doesn't mean that all the weapons were taken over but only some of it. And it is not hidden. This is written down in order to be aware of who is using the weapons, and they, when they took the weapons, nobody made sure to control that and they are the ones who fired those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's interesting, Mr. Krsman. So you're saying a decision was passed and you're insisting on the significance of that to establish a full unit with the weapons that were taken over under the direction of the NSC and then you want to assert that when the weapons were used, they were used by people who were not under control. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me. It says what we are going to do with the weapons that the Serbs took, and as for the weapons that were taken by the Muslims, those weapons were out of control and those are the weapons that were used to fire at us and hence problems in Smajici [phoen] and the ones that the two people are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, but Gagovic is talking about weapons from Faletici being used to shell and destroy Sokolje. Are you suggesting that Sokolje was shelled and destroyed by the weapons taken by the Muslims and that's what Gagovic was saying to Smajic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The one does not have anything to do with the other. So Sokolje was hit it was not razed to the ground and those are two totally different terms. Fire was opened on Sokolje as a result of previous attacks. It was a deterrent. On the 8th of May, Jelica Boro was killed and it says in the conversation that Mirko Krajisnik wanted to express his condolences. Mr. Miletic is a Croat. He was the commander of the barracks. There was the JNA in the barracks, and I absolutely stand by my statement. We opened fire on the suburbs of Sokolje and Brescevo [phoen] and that was the only thing we did as a deterrent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, Your Honour, that we bordered on Sokolje so we targeted just those trenches that they have dug and I already said on the 8th of May they already had trenches and communicating trenches from which they targeted us. So we used infantry weapons, whereas the barracks, according to the rules of military service, until they -- there was probably an attack, an infantry attack, on the barracks and Colonel Miletic knows this, and that's not contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- were weapons used that were taken from Faletici in this deterrent action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That's quite a different -- Faletici is quite a different part of town and you have to go 150 kilometres round about to reach Rajlovac, so that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether you know whether these were weapons from Faletici. You seem to indicate that on the basis of logic, that you exclude for that possibility. Do you know where those weapons came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the barracks had weapons which it had at its disposal and I said when we took the rifle from the barracks we didn't know what remained in the barracks so usually three-barreled weapons were used, mortars, and cannons of 40-millimetre calibre because that's what the army had in the Rajlovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, this is a contemporaneous phone call by Mr. Smajic to Gagovic begging to have this shelling stopped because hundreds of homes have already been destroyed and people are huddled in their shelters begging for help. Are you suggesting this didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the conversation, it says that it was a synchronised attack on the part of the Muslims and that Hadzici were attacked. Look at it this way: This conversation was shown on the news bulletin and the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina heard this conversation. It was broadcast on television. And Mr. Smajic worked in propaganda for the Muslim side. I understand that. That's quite normal but it's also quite understandable that the people from Sokolje who had an agreement with us until the 8th of May, then it was quite understand that they were astounded how the extremists had infiltrated their ranks and had provoked them. So the army, of course, had to respond and this is just proof and evidence that everything I've said so far I said correctly, that it was the truth. And had this not happened, on their part, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina would never have started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that it was a long answer. Do I have to understand this to say that it did not happen, what Mr. Smajic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened but not with that scope and not targeted features but just as response to their provocation. You see, when the commander says that the -- they were targeted from Boljokov and Brijesce by mortars, these are mobile mortars just to create panic and legitimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. You say it did happen, not on that scale and it was provoked. Now, in the telephone conversation, it is said that 250 out of 300 houses were destroyed in Sokolje. To what extent is that true, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know and what is then the correct level of destruction, if there was any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 90 per cent of the shells up to 40-millimetre calibre was in the first line of battle. Part of the shells probably fall -- fell far of their target because the men were not trained sufficiently. And the next day or the day after, when I took my binoculars to have a look you couldn't notice anything at all. You couldn't in the any destruction whatsoever. But it's quite normal that at the beginning of the war, and 95 per cent of us didn't hear a cannon being fired let alone see it, and Mr. Smajic himself says that he didn't leave the television station for four days. How can he know what happened? Whereas here it says he's -- he talks about all this destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said already that it was not true, so his source of knowledge is implicitly disputed by you. You say there was no damage at all, then, or since you said -- it's still not clear. He says 250 houses out of 300. Do you say none, 50, 100, 200? I do understand that you consider this to be collateral damage rather than targeting but how many houses were destroyed according to your knowledge, or if you don't know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that not a single house was destroyed. When you say destroyed house it means the house that has been completely razed and that you can't live it in any more. Of course, some were damaged by the shells but I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but I'm talking about so heavily damaged that it's difficult or impossible to continue living there. None of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guarantee that up until August, not a single house was destroyed. That is to say, destroyed to that extent that it couldn't be lived in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, in your earlier testimony, you described Sokolje as an area with more than 90 per cent women, children, elderly and students. Now you're telling us that Sokolje was shelled in a way so that -- by people who didn't even know precisely or even remotely where the shells were going. Isn't it true, Mr. Krsman, that when you were responding to the Judge's questions on Friday, about the evil that was done to the Serbs by the Muslims, and the evil that was done to the Muslims by the Serbs, that when you said at page 76 of the LiveNote, "I don't know how many people were killed at shock lay," this is precisely the kind of thing you were referring to, the massive disproportionate, undirected shelling of the civilian area.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all I did not say that Sokolje was made up 90 per cent of women and children. On the basis of the population census I said that every family had quite considerable -- a quite considerable number of children, more than us, that's point number 1. Point number 2 is this: We never targeted civilian targets. Never. And I stand by that. I was the commander of the company, and Sokolje was tied up with my unit. We never targeted civilian targets, except in the case of where cannons or mortars were next to a facility and feature then that is no longer civilian, that is a legitimate military target then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also asserted, if I understood you correctly, that no houses were severely damaged. Let me turn your attention to tab 24, which is a SRNA press release from 11 May 1992, with the thirds paragraph indicating in the night of 9 May the Green Berets and HOS launched an attack on Rajlovac barracks on which occasion they also burned down Sokolje. So SRNA seems to think that Sokolje suffered some pretty significant destruction, Mr. Krsman, only they want to blame it on the Muslims. But as you've just told us, it was Serb forces which shelled Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the journalist wanted to say but what I said is very clear. Now, what he meant by saying that they burnt Sokolje, perhaps he wanted to say that they initiated their attack on us. I don't know what he wanted to say by that. You would have to ask him because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unless the Court has any questions I'm going to move to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time, Mr. Tieger, how much time would have you in mind, looking at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please move to your next subject and finish before the next break. By the way, Mr. Tieger, I had some difficulties in finding the minutes of the Council for National Security under P65, 30. I do find it under P433 although with a different translation. Translation is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, you're quite right and I read from the wrong -- I read from the portion below it. It's P433.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you may have noticed that the translation you're providing now is not exactly the same as the -- perhaps you review that and see what is -- whether you'd like us to look at the first one or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will do precisely that, Your Honour, and if I may, I won't finish without taxing the endurance of the interpreting staff. If this is a convenient moment for the Court, before I move on to the last subject, I would suggest we take a break since we are so close to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually we sit for close to first session one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The court is right. We started late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started late at approximately 2.30 so therefore we are now at 1 hour ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you testified in your examination-in-chief that during the time you were living in Mr. Krajisnik's home in the late 80s, his level of participation in the events in -- his political participation was at the local level. You recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wasn't living in his house, as it says in the translation. I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's my mistake, and thank you for that clarification. That is, of course, what you said during your examination-in-chief. Now, thereafter, after Mr. Krajisnik assumed political responsibilities at the republic level, Serbs from Rajlovac continued to seek his guidance and direction and he continued to provide it, correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the sphere of the tasks already started, as president of the Socialist Alliance of the working people, with respect to the utilities, the buses, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware he became involved in the establishment, the discussions concerning the establishment of the Rajlovac municipality and its splitting off from the Novi Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just like all of us. He was just one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't really place your significance in those discussions at the same level as Mr. Krajisnik's would you?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, for example, tab 14, reflects a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Koljevic in February 1992, in which Mr. Krajisnik relates about halfway down through the first page, that he has a meeting in Rajlovac in connection with this one municipality, and then on the last page he continues that he thought of going down to tell you those peasants of mine are waiting for me. People want to talk to me so I said that I will come. And similarly in tab 15, we see a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic and I believe that needs a number, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In which Mr. Krajisnik tells Dr. Karadzic that -- well, as it says he's not. "He's gone down to Reljevo. So down there, people, I'm right. I have one. Big territory. They want to establish Rajlovac municipality as it used to be, you know." Dr. Karadzic responds, "Uh-huh." Mr. Krajisnik continues, "That's a big territory so then people want to sit down with them. I stayed until late last night and I had to go to the constitutional commission so I asked Milos to go. I can't." That Milos Savic. So those are further reflections of the efforts by Mr. Krajisnik in connection with the establishment of Rajlovac municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That simply isn't a question, Your Honour. Let me correct that. It is a question but it's not a question that this witness can sensibly or seriously answer. It's a device and not a very well hidden one, in my respectful submission, to introduce this additional evidence. It's simply not something Mr. Krsman can realistically deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May the witness remove his earphones, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take your ear phones off, Mr. Krsman?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, no device, as Mr. Josse refers to it, I think with a condemning intent, is necessary in this situation. Such evidence would be appropriate based on the evidence elicited by the defence. Beyond that, it's the Prosecution's contention precisely as put to the witness, and the witness is in a position to affirm or contradict it, since he was present at the time, involved in these efforts to the extent he described it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's a bit difficult for a witness to know what was said in a telephone conversation. But Mr. Tieger, I think it would -- you could confront the witness with the existence of a telephone conversation between, as it appears, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, on which they discuss that Milos Savic would go to Reljevo in relation to the establishment of Rajlovac municipality, whether the witness is aware that Mr. Savic went there. I mean these are facts. But we can't ask the witness, apart from whether this could be a document which could be admitted as a contextual document, I mean that would be something to be considered if you would ask for that, but I think it's not a right way of doing if the witness isn't aware of such a telephone conversation to ask him whether this is an example of involvement of Mr. Krajisnik in the local level. I think we should stick to, then, specific facts rather than referring to telephone conversation the witness is not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean we are refining, it seems to me, our methods of presentation and introduction of evidence. I just want to make it completely clear that the introduction of an intercept of this nature in response to the evidence elicited by the Defence is completely appropriate and precisely the kind of document which the Court should have. If there are ways in which the Court prefer that be presented of course I'm -- I want to respond to that but I don't think there is any question that this is the kind of information that the Court should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I gave you some guidance on what you could ask the witness perhaps in relation to this document, since it appeared to us that there were -- especially at the beginning of this document, seemed to have relevance to you. The Chamber has no preference in that respect. The Chamber will decide on any objection raised by Mr. Josse. He raised an objection. I give you guidance to deal with that. If you think that it's important for the Chamber to have this document available, then I leave it to your inventivity on how to present it and then we'll hear from Mr. Josse whether that's a correct way of presenting it, yes or no. He at least objected to the way you introduced it now and I gave you the guidance on how deal with it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, prior to the establishment of the Rajlovac municipality, did the political authorities, Serbian political authorities in Rajlovac, express an interest in meeting with Dr. Karadzic in connection with the establishment or the proposed establishment of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't need Dr. Karadzic or anybody else for that matter. We as a people proceeded according to the constitution and our rights under it. Why would we need Dr. Karadzic? He wasn't an inhabitant of ours, nor had I ever met him or seen him in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, could you please answer the question? The question was whether the authorities expressed an interest in meeting with Dr. Karadzic. Just tell us whether they expressed such an interest, yes or no. Sometime people do express an interest in something they do not need. Sometimes people do not express any interest in matters they might need. So the logic and the explanations, please tell us whether ever such an expression of interest -- whether the Serbian political authorities in Rajlovac expressed an interest in meeting with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no. Did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. But I take it that you're not disputing that others apart from you or apart from those people to whom you may have spoken about this matter expressed such an interest in meeting with Dr. Karadzic, conveyed through Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say I don't know. If I knew, I would tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, after the establishment of the Rajlovac municipality and after the outbreak of the conflict, it is correct, isn't it, that Mr. Krajisnik continued to have a significant role in events in the Rajlovac municipality? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that he had but he didn't have any role. He had his state affairs to attend to, not to deal with Rajlovac. We took it upon ourselves to solve all the problems that cropped up after the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take a look, then, at tab 18, please. You've looked at tab 18 before. These are the remarks by -- I'm sorry we didn't. My mistake. These are the remarks by Mr. Trifko Radic whom we have discussed before, this time, at the RS assembly held in Bijeljina on 14 and 15 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger it appears as with a number on the list. This verbatim record of the 20th session of the Republika Srpska assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'll take a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to look at my other list, compare the list -- Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, if you'll take a look at your page 48, and go down to the last two sentences of that first paragraph, which end in a long ellipsis or "..." Where Mr. Radic says, "The Ustasha attack us on all fronts every day, we have no help. I went to see Mr. Krajisnik and General Mladic and if they hadn't come, we would have fallen a long time ago. If Ilijas falls, so will Rajlovac, Vogosca, and others." I'm sorry, Your Honour, in English that's at page 46?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Bottom of 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That, Mr. Krsman, is a reflection of Mr. Krajisnik's role when major issues concerning Rajlovac and the surrounding areas were at stake, such as the need for military help in the face of an enemy attack, correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. You asked me about Rajlovac. Ilijas is 30 kilometres away from Rajlovac. I don't know whether Mr. Krajisnik went to Rajlovac. You'll have to ask him. And as for Ilijas -- sorry, Rajlovac, he didn't come to Rajlovac. I told you when he was in Rajlovac last. We did not expect him to help us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that seems strikes as a potentially fine distinction but because you made it let's look at Rajlovac specifically and in that connection I would like you to turn to tab 9. Tab 9, which needs a number, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is a 12 December 1992 strictly confidential report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. And at item number 5 it reports an unusual incident related to problems with the Rajlovac command, commander, and Chief of Staff, and so on. Talks about the measures that would be needed to resolve and settle the situation, including the establishment of authorities that will cooperate with the command staff and work on achieving the goals of the Serbian people's war. And in that connection, the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps request an urgent meeting with Trifko Radic, whom we've talked about before, the president of Rajlovac and Vogosca and President Krajisnik. And that, sir, is a reflection of the importance of Mr. Krajisnik's role related to Rajlovac as a political figure to whom both military and political officials turned in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I repeat the objection I made earlier. It's exactly the same point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the time frame should be clear. We are now talking about December 1992, from what I understand. What -- you could ask the witness whether he knows anything about any involvement at that point in time of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, were you aware of the fact that officials at this level turned to Mr. Krajisnik under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is 12 December 1992. On the 9 December 1992, the Muslim formations launched an offensive against Zuc. Our line fell in the depth up to five kilometres, and that is why this is entitled, unusual incident and this is all I know about this date. The command asked for a new line to be set up since we had lost some of the territory, they wanted us to -- and I don't know anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was not whether what happened exactly on the front line at that moment but the question was about people at a certain level calling for the intervention and if you would say under those circumstances, it's understandable or I'm not aware of it, fine, but are you aware of in relation to that moment and perhaps the events that took place at that time, of any call for Mr. Krajisnik to intervene or to -- well, to get involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything. I only know what I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, ten minutes, you said before. That's far beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not a very good estimator sometimes, Your Honour. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, we gave you already quite some more. Therefore, I said whether you would like -- I invited you to finish by the next break and it's time for the next break now so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One last question, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you simply don't know about the level of contact between people reflected in this order and Mr. Krajisnik, isn't that right, during the course of 1992? You just don't know that.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And I was not supposed to know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Josse I take it after the break you would like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do have some questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to begin my re-examination, Mr. Krsman, with the very last question that you were asked by my learned friend, Mr. Tieger. He asked you we put to you that you don't know the level of contact between people reflected in the document that he had just presented and Mr. Krajisnik, and you said, "I don't know and I was not supposed to know anything about that." What did you mean when you said, "And I was not supposed to know anything about that"?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war started we all had our own tasks. I had my own tasks which was to defend the line and I dedicated my time to that task. Those who were in the rear tended to their tasks, what I meant was that I was not supposed to have any contacts or do anything else that did not concern my task, which was to defend the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at the document that you were referred to at tab 9. Are you able to assist the Chamber as to whether Mr. Krajisnik did in fact attend the meeting that commander Galic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, your question suggests that the meeting took place. It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In my mind, any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour would be wrong to come to that conclusion. First of all, because I'm -- because I'm not -- I'm unable to lead, I couldn't put anything to the witness even if I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No but nevertheless you are you able to assist the Chamber as too whether Mr. Krajisnik did in fact attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, referring to in the future could be the meeting or a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I should have said any meeting. It certainly was not my intention to suggest that such a meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore I just seek clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked the following question earlier today: When you wouldn't really place your significance in those discussions at the same level as Mr. Krajisnik's, would you? And you said, well, of course, not. And the discussions that were you being asked about were those relating to the establishment of the Rajlovac municipality and its splitting off from Novi Grad. What was your significance in those discussions, please, Mr. Krsman?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krajisnik is older than me. Second of all, I was the president of the association of youth and I attended those meetings as anybody else. When Mr. Krajisnik took up another duty he was replaced by somebody else. And within that context I said that I was not on par with Mr. Krajisnik. Otherwise, we had the same right to propose things, to elect people, to adopt decisions and conclusions. In that respect we were on an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were also asked earlier today at the end of a long question, about the -- and I quote, "The massive, disproportionate, undirected shelling of the civilian area." Referring to the matters raised in the long intercept that we heard, what do you say to the allegation that you were involved in, I quote again, "Massive, disproportionate, undirected shelling of the civilian area"?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fire was controlled by one part of the JNA that had remained in the barracks. The fire was calibre from 20 to 40 millimetre and we only had light weapons and we were not in a position to inflict any alleged damages on the facilities. As for what happened next, I said when the army had -- once had been established, then we assumed all the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the long intercept is concerned, do you accept what Mr. Smajic was saying to Mr. Gagovic? In other words, was his account of matters in accordance with your recollection as to what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that is correct is when he said that they had provoked and for two shells we responded inappropriately. It was not two shells that were fired. Next to my house, there are still to this day some 50 holes done by mortar shells, one of them killing my neighbour. Between 200 and 300 shells fell on that village and the shelling continued until the moment that this conversation was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Earlier today, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just to avoid whatever confusion, that village is, you say? Between 200 and 300 shells fell on that village. What village were you exactly referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My village, around my house. My house was closest to the separation line, and some 50 shells fell close to it, and in depth of the territory towards Zabrdje some 200 shells fell on that evening, on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In an answer you gave earlier, in relation to this intercept, you said, "This conversation was shown on the news bulletin and the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina heard this conversation. It was broadcast on television. And Mr. Smajic worked in propaganda for the Muslim side. I understand that." Firstly are you saying that this precise intercept was on television?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Smajic was the editor of a daily, the title of which was YUTEL as an acronym of something that starts with U [as interpreted] for Yugoslavia. Similar conversation, maybe not this one, but similar conversations did take place at first but later on they sided with the Muslim side because Mr. Smajic was a Muslim and another person called Gordan Milic was on the same team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Take this slowly, please, Mr. Krsman. When you talk about him working in propaganda and this being propaganda, explain exactly what you mean about this conversation being propaganda. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all you have to know that all Serbs had abandoned the broadcasting house. Mr. Smajic here belittles the intervention of Muslims. He starts to portray their provocations and shelling as being to a lesser extent than it was. But in the forefront is non-selective shelling of non-military targets. This is his first lie. And he himself said that he had friends in the barracks and they would have known who had shelled them and I'm sure that somebody else would have called in addition to him. But what I'm saying is that he was part of the propaganda and that he tried to exaggerate incidents even when -- where those incidents did not take place at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And by exaggerating incidents or indeed describing incidents that did not take place at all, in a conversation with a gentleman like Mr. Gagovic, what, as you understand it, would be his purpose? What would he -- what would he be trying to achieve in terms of propaganda benefit?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his goal was. Rajlovac is over 7 or 8 kilometres away from the television, and the colonel said that the shells had a range of 3.000 metres. There was so much propaganda that one could no longer tolerate it. Everything was blamed on Serbs, and Serbs were not to be blamed for anything. And I believe that this was the only reason that he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no questions, thank you. Your Honour, I am -- there was one lingering matter from Friday that wasn't addressed and that was the issue of the letters that didn't -- it was actually the first exhibit or first tab to which I turned the witness's attention during my examination. Those were the three letters, one of which didn't correspond with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the companies. The companies becoming four, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under P1131 and 1132 and P1133.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the incorrect -- well, there was a correct translation but an incorrect original. In any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least they did not match.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's exactly right. Here are the complete sets. I don't know how the Court wishes to handle it but we could certainly give them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I would like to do -- I take it that the witness only saw the B/C/S ones. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure he had all three of them from recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think 1 and 3 were shown to him and he nevertheless -- he said something about the second one. He mentioned the name of the second company. So therefore I would suggest that we'll proceed as far as admission is concerned on the basis of the three we had in front of us, that was Vemex, that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists Mr. Josse in particular, and perhaps the Court, the -- I read the -- I think almost all of the Vemex letter which was the problem letter. I think the witness heard that translation but in the course of reviewing the documents in the tab also saw the other letters. So if he commented I actually don't recall specifically at this moment. On Vemex, that was no doubt in response to the translation that was provided from the English, that indeed corresponds to the letter we now have in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm content with the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- if Your Honour is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll check it again on the transcript but I'm for the time being I'm happy with the situation as well. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I would have a few questions for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, did you ever learn about events that happened in a village Ahatovici? And I'm specifically asking about what happened to the Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is what I heard from other people. That was a village where Muslims constituted a relative majority. It was close to the Butile barracks, which is a remote barracks in Dobrosevici, and I know that there was an ultimatum and that some fighting ensued. Following the ultimatum some of them were killed, the others were captured. Later on they were exchanged, and this is all I know about this incident. This was at the far end on the opposite side to my zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say "ultimatum," what do you mean by that, ultimatum to do what or not to do what?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the ultimatum was to free a passage for them to go to Sarajevo, around the clock. And I believe that the command could not grant that. And then they attacked the Butile barracks. Fighting ensued. There were casualties on both sides. And what happened next was the way I described it in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From whom did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that on the line, as people were coming back, there were a lot of refugees from that area, some of whom ended up on my line of defence and I heard it from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said some of them were captured. Do you know anything about the circumstances under which they were held in detention?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that they were kept between 3 and 7 days. Somewhere either in the barracks or somewhere else. And those were only men. And after seven days, they were either exchanged or taken to be exchanged. This is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever learn about an incident where detained people that were detained in Rajlovac died in a bus when leaving Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that incident, which took place somewhere around Srenje some 30 or 40 kilometres away from Rajlovac.
