According to the story that I heard, the bus was intercepted by Muslim formations because they thought that the bus was full of our soldiers. There were some casualties, both Serbs and Muslims, but I don't know whether this is all true because where this happened was no man's land. It was not controlled either by the Muslims or by the Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Finally, last question: Your line was I would say on the slopes of Zuc hill. Is that -- or would you not consider that Zuc hill?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line was in the zone of responsibility after the Rajlovac Brigade and this line was manned by the locals of Zuc. Out of 358, while they were manning it, when Zuc fell on the 9th of September, that line disappeared and these people were deployed and they were assigned to other platoons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this Chamber has received some evidence on Muslims being taken to Zuc to perform work obligations where some of them were injured, some of them died. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility, nobody came, no other people came except for the people who were there. As for Zuc I really can't say. I don't know. If they were, then each person must be held responsible for their actions during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any questions arising from questions from the Bench? If not, Mr. Krsman, this completes your testimony in this Court. You've answered the questions put to you by both parties and by the Bench. I'd like to thank you for coming the far distance to The Hague and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Krsman out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first say the following to the parties. I think I used in response to an objection raised by you, Mr. Josse, the word "to confront the witness with" I think twice, where I -- that's perhaps my lack of knowledge of the English language, where I intended to use a softer language, and I should have preferred finally to say "to put that to a witness." The difference in my language were where the word confront also exists is a bit smaller. Where the verb to confront may have been misunderstood, it was not directly related to the witness but it was I think when I gave guidance to you, Mr. Tieger, I intended to say to put something to a witness rather than to confront the witness with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could we deal with the exhibits right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, we have the exhibits. I think new ones go -- range from P1131 up to and including P1137. Any objections, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask about the position with 1135? And I appreciate that this may have happened in the case before but some clarification even now perhaps wouldn't go amiss. Leave aside the -- that is the intercept between my client and Radovan Karadzic in February of 1992. Leave aside for one moment, if the Court would be so kind, my objection as to the nature of the questioning and the way that it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Only the first two remarks of my client were introduced in evidence. What we need to know is whether those are the only two remarks that are going to be read by the Chamber in relation to this document. I know this is an old chestnut nut, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly we did not find time to read the remainder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, to what extent is the remainder of that telephone conversation relevant or did you just present it in order to not deprive us from the context in which it was said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I would urge -- I would argue that -- first of all let me step back. I accept that there are circumstances in which directing a witness's attention to only a portion of the document may mean for a variety of reasons that the remainder of the document should not be admitted. I don't need to describe to the Court examples we've had of that. I don't think an intercepted telephone conversation of this length falls into that category. Now, the extent of -- the weight to be given the remainder of that conversation depends, has always, on a variety of circumstances, and in particular, the totality of the evidence that might otherwise relate to it, but this is a conversation that I think should be admitted in its entirety both to understand the nature of the comments and context of the comments related to Rajlovac, and indeed for other such purposes as it may usefully serve, given the totality of the evidence. Clearly, that portion which is focused at the time of its introduction presumably has its own independent added weight for that reason. But I submit that the remainder of the conversation also has evidential value which should not be kept from the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then perhaps not introduced through there witness. That's, I take it, the issue, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the second issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the second issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: An issue with respect I was going to raise in any event. Perhaps dealing with the second issue, I invite the Court to consider carefully what Mr. Tieger said at the bottom of page 31 of today's LiveNote where, in effect, in my submission, he conceded the very point of my objection, namely, and I'll put it in a rather contentious way, I accept, by using the word "device," but he accepted that it was a way of presenting and introducing evidence. And the Court -- as Your Honour observed to him in the course of argument, in effect needs to grapple with that method of presentation that the Prosecution are adopting. And bearing in mind Mr. Tieger's concession, we submit at page 31, it would be wrong now to admit this intercept into evidence. So that's the second point. The first point is whether the rest of the document should go in in any event. And our fall back position is that if the Court is against the Defence and that it should be admitted, it should only be admitted in part and those first ten lines or so which end with Mr. Krajisnik saying the words, "Milos Savic" should be admitted and no more than that. I hope I make the Defence position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The position is quite clear. Of course, one of the -- I've not read the whole of it yet. I take it my colleagues neither. There, of course, is always the risk of whether we start reading it if we don't have to read it, if they are talking about the weather for the remainder of the telephone conversation which, of course, I do not expect because they had other things to discuss at that time I take it, then, of course, the parties could agree upon it. If, however, the importance because -- Mr. Tieger, you were rather vague on should not be kept from the Court but I've got no idea if I would ask you now to summarise the remainder of it I wonder whether you would be in a position to do that right away, whether you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I might be cheating, Your Honour, since it's in front of me. Let me point out, however, I'm not aware of intending to make any concession. I just looked at my remarks. I don't think I inadvertently made a concession along the lines the Defence suggest so I would prefer at least there is no implicit acknowledgement that that was done on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be possible that the parties for the remainder of the text -- of course, we still have to consider about the first I would say ten to 15 lines, if the remainder, of which Mr. Tieger says it should not be kept from us, is not that important, he could consider whether it would be really so dramatic to keep that away from us. At the same time, Mr. Josse, you're invited the remainder of the -- of the telephone conversation would not do any damage whatsoever to your case, to see whether you could resolve the matter between yourselves. If not we will read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I mention one other matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The reason in relation to this -- the reason that the matter is a sensitive one to me personally, and I suspect my client as well, is I've been tasked with trying to deal with intercepts in preparation for his evidence, and there are a vast number of intercepts. A significant number involve him. We are trying to go through all of those. And one of the things we have to grapple with and to some extent the Court will have to grapple with, is how many of those Mr. Krajisnik realistically needs to deal with personally because if a matter has been introduced into evidence, it's a matter that we will stand upon at a later stage. But I flag it up now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Josse. At the same time I'm quite frank to you: I've got no idea what the remainder of the conversation is about. If finally we would have to decide and by reading it we have to establish that that's just about the weather, then I wonder why it was so important not to keep away the weather from us and what -- how it would be so important for the Defence to -- not to be informed about the matter. You understand what I mean? I'm just trying to see whether there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do but, of course, as Your Honour observed, that point cuts both ways --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- between both the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I fully accept the Court's suggestion. I will be more than happy to undertake the initial steps and that will presumably prevent or obviate any need for Mr. Josse to undertake any further efforts until he hears from me. So I think we have an excellent chance of resolving this without the Court's intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's great. Otherwise we will give a decision on the matter. Apart, of course, the lines that remain are still to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I made my submission about those. I have nothing else. I have no objection to any of the other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None of the others, so then apart from P1135, the exhibits are admitted into evidence. Then Defence Exhibits, Mr. Tieger, they range from D153 up to and including D156. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then they are admitted into evidence. I have a few more procedural issues still on our list which we could deal with very rapidly, I take it. Yes. First of all, the Nielsen exhibits, the footnote material. The Chamber would like to address the parties regarding the Nielsen source material. On the 8th of March, and I'm referring to pages 20902 to 20903, the Chamber requested that the Prosecution determine the availability of parts of the Nielsen's reports source material making reference to three groups of documents. On the 14th of March, and I refer to transcript pages 21266 to 270, the Prosecution informed the Chamber of the availability of the requested material. In light of the Chamber's remarks to the party regarding this material on the 15th of March, transcript pages 21453 to 21454, and the subsequent Defence request for clarification filed on the 17th of March, the Chamber would now like to revisit the matter. Notwithstanding the rather -- and now I think I use the word as it is meant -- the rather confrontational tone of the Defence request for clarification, a request which could easily have been made by the Defence at the time the Chamber gave its decision. The Chamber would like to resolve this matter quickly and proceed along a more traditional course in dealing with the Nielsen source material. The Chamber would like to remind the parties of the guidance it offered on the procedure for examining expert witnesses on the 5th of May 2005, set forth beginning on transcript page 13085. The Chamber informed the parties under point 5 of its guidance that, "All remaining documentation underlying the experts report will not be admitted into evidence unless one of the parties showing good cause in light of the above or the Chamber itself specifically requests so." The Chamber has reserved the discretion to request documentation underlying an expert report, thus allowing it to verify facts underlying the conclusion made by experts. The Chamber hereby orders the Prosecution to submit for admission into evidence the group of documents cited in the Nielsen report which, according to the Republika Srpska MUP draft annual report for 1992, were received by the Presidency. The Defence is given two weeks from the date of submission of these documents to raise any objections. The Chamber requests the Prosecution to submit their documents in court at an appropriate moment at which time they will be assigned provisional exhibit numbers. The Chamber is not requesting at this time submission of the group of documents which were purportedly received by the Prime Minister or the group of issues of the bulletin daily events. The Chamber will inform the Prosecution if it later wishes to request the submission of these documents. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Next point, I don't know who to address, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Harmon, the Chamber received a request for protective measures for a witness who will testify soon. If there is any need to respond to this request we would like to hear your response no later than Thursday but if you can give an oral response now, but if you would need to go into private session, then please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've notified the Defence, Your Honour, that we intend to respond in writing and we will do so by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Then, Mr. Josse, any objections to the Lakic exhibits which were to be lodged by today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've been discussing that and corresponding by e-mail with Mr. Margetts. My concern, Your Honour, is in relation to P1112. This was the -- described as an extract from Radovan Karadzic's diary. At the time, the Chamber, following a request from me, this is my recollection, at least, were given a brief history of how the Office of the Prosecutor came by this particular document, and as such, we have no difficulty with that. The difficulty lies, as to whether it can be attributed to Mr. Karadzic and whether it in fact is his diary. Now, my vague recollection is - excuse me for not having checked this specifically - was that the witness accepted what was put to him as to what was contained within the diary, and that was Mr. Margetts's recollection when I discussed the matter with him earlier today. So there is no problem as such with that extract being admitted into evidence but at this stage, the Defence would ask the Chamber and indeed the Prosecution not to jump to the conclusion that it is in fact Karadzic's diary. It's accepted that the Prosecution say that it was seized from Mrs. Karadzic's home in the course of the spring of last year, just May of last year, when it was raided by NATO troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But beyond that at this stage, we would invite the Chamber to go no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd say you do not oppose admission to evidence the witness has testified about it but not to take it for granted that by the place where it was found and by the testimony of this witness, that would also justify the conclusion that it was Mr. Karadzic's handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is our submission. I should add in fairness to the Prosecution, they served it upon us about three weeks ago so we have had a chance to consider it. Mr. Krajisnik in particular has had a chance to scrutinise it. But in effect, putting it another way, an old common law way we would put the Prosecution to proof of the fact that it was written by Karadzic, if that be their assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I had a response before I was challenged to consider it in the classical common law way but what I wanted to say before that is given my understanding of the status of the discussions between Mr. Margetts and Josse, it seems to me that's a fair reservation on the part of the Defence. For the time being the document comes in as a document that was seized in a manner he described and from the place he described and the discussions continue, if necessary, on the remaining point that he raised. If there comes a point at which that issue needs to be resoled by the Court then I think we can bra it to the attention of the court at that time. Meanwhile the status remains as described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it seems that that's a fair reflection of the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are agreed, up until this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, anything else on the Lakic exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then they range from P1109 up to and including P1117, and are admitted into evidence as far as Defence exhibits are concerned, Mr. Tieger, I don't know whether you can respond or whether we need Mr. Margetts for it. It would go from D146 up to and including D149. If you'd say I'll consult with Mr. Margetts we'll hear, then we'll give you another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We would appreciate that opportunity, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No decision has been taken on the Defence exhibits. Finally, yes, we have the issue of what I would call the Hotic documents. The Prosecution on the 24th of March were ready to tender these documents but that the Defence would have to look at it first. According to what I understand has been presented as a kind of an informal deadline, the 28th of March was set.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I had a chance to review these with the translations, and whilst as the Chamber is an I wear, the Defence has serious reservations about the procedure that the Chamber has adopted, in this case, we do not oppose the admission of these documents. Could I repeat, I may have said on a previous occasion, we are trying as best we can to make our own inquiries in relation to this matter. However, it is -- the authenticity of the documents isn't seriously in dispute. Those that have been translated can, as far as we are concerned, go before the Court. I was provided with a helpful introductory note by Mr. Harmon. I would invite that that does not, however, go to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let them do their own work, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not -- of course, I do not know the content of it. It was helpful for you, whether it would be helpful for us or not, we have our own --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I rather walked into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Harmon, may I then take it that you'll tender the documents one of these days without the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour we can tender them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, the complete Hotic file I have in my possession. I have had translated probably 98 per cent of the documents. There are some documents that obviously had no bearing or relevance whatsoever. I provided the Defence with a complete inventory and all of the documents in B/C/S and all of the translated documents in English, so counsel has had an opportunity to review all of the translations. I provided counsel, as he has said, with a complete set of English translations and I'm prepared to submit now the Hotic file, those documents from that file that have been selected by me and that have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then take it, Mr. Josse, that if there are any untranslated documents are therefore not tendered at this moment which the Defence would consider to be relevant, that you'll ask for completion of this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour we can tender them right now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you could give it to Mr. Registrar and then see how numbering will proceed, whether we do it in one number with subnumbers or that depends a bit also on -- so I invite the Registrar not to immediately assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just look at one of those bundles, please, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It does have the very note that I was -- that's the very note that I was objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hotic case, KT-460, 04.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the very note I was objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Immediately, Mr. Harmon, I take it that this was not a slip of the pen but a slip of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Copier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Slip of your hand in --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That note is merely an inventory for counsel's use of what documents he was provided with, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We might make an inventory. If it's just an inventory, Mr. Josse, and without any comment, then you might be in a position to reconsider whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will consider the matter between now and 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we will not put them in the shredder yet. Mr. Registrar is keeping a close eye on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I assure the Court I will reread it between now and the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And then perhaps also today, Mr. Registrar will form an opinion and how best to number these exhibits. There are no other procedural issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojovic informs me that he handed to Mr. Haider four documents earlier today, all of which have already got numbers. They comply with orders that the Chamber has previously made in relation to Defence documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I sincerely hope they have got to my learned friends, the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least they have clear numbers on it. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is nothing else that I wish to raise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we have a break now so that with your next witness you would have -- you could examine the next witness without any interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart has the pleasure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until ten minutes to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's Mrs. Svetlana Cenic, no protective measures, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cenic, before you give evidence in this Court the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth and I'd first of all like to ask you whether you want to make that solemn declaration in your own language or in English, because I understand that you are, as you just showed, you're fluent in English. I leave it up to you which you prefer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will give the statement in my own language, in the Serb language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would -- Madam Usher, would you please give the text of the solemn declaration to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, please be seated, Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to tell Mrs. Cenic that she'll first be examined by you, Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just going to say, Mrs. Cenic, as she did the solemn declaration she will be giving her evidence in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it entirely to her. And I can imagine that you feel most at ease to use your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic to begin with, because I feel confident there won't be any objection I'm going to put a number of facts to you and invite your agreement so that we can get fairly quickly through areas which one doesn't suppose are likely to be in contention. The -- so I'll put it to you in chunks and you can tell the Court if you agree or if there is anything you want to correct. You were born on the 6th of December 1960 in Sarajevo, you graduated from degree in economics in Sarajevo, you have at various times worked in Belgrade and in England but you returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina to work within the last few years, is that correct, and when did you go back there last?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I returned from England as somebody who had worked for two English companies as their representative. However, very soon all the investments stopped, the company that I worked for were engaged in investment. I had to return to Sarajevo. I could not keep my family in England and this was sometime in 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So then in 1991, you were working in Sarajevo as an economic consultant with some British companies. In April 1992, in circumstances which we'll come back to, it's correct, that you were forced to move with your family from Sarajevo, you arrived in Vogosca on the 15th of April 1992, you lived there until early July 1992, when you moved to Pale; is that right so far?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. With a correction. My parents left on the 4th of April, hoping that they would return. They just went for a weekend to my grandmother's place and I myself managed to reenter Sarajevo on several occasions until the 15th of April, after which date it was impossible either to enter Sarajevo or leave it if you were already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, I'm going to ask you to put your ear phones on. I do understand that you do understand English. If -- they will fall off again and again if you don't put -- the reason why I'm asking you is that the interpreters might sooner or later have a problem with your speed of speech. I noticed already that -- I take it then that you -- yes, of course, if you're using the B/C/S channel it doesn't help that much but if you want to listen to the questions in English, then, of course, you will also -- or perhaps you could also listen to the live channel which is channel 3, I think, because if you speak too quickly and you may be familiar with the problem, then the interpreters might have problems in following you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's helpful, Your Honour. We think channel 3 does the trick for this purpose. Let's try it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic I'm just going through, if you like, your -- very briefly your biography over the last few years and then we'll come back to Pale but in the autumn of 1992, still in Pale, you started working in the office of the vice-president -- I beg your pardon, of Dr. Nikola Koljevic as his personal assistant?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you remained in his office and he became the vice-president, didn't he, until August 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After that, you moved to Banja Luka where you worked as an economic consultant until 2000 and then from December 2000 until October 2002, you were an adviser to the vice-president of Republika Srpska, is that all correct so far?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then from October 2002 until February 2005, you were an adviser to the president of the -- of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then until a change of government at the end of last month, February 2006, you had been the Minister of Finance of the -- of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you have just recently then -- following that change of government, you have accepted a position as a -- the director or manager of the European centre for peace and development, which is under the aegis of the University of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mrs. Cenic, you've never -- you are not now and you never have been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Not only of the SDS. I have never been a member of any political party in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I ask you now, when did you first meet Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, whom you see in court here today?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: In 1991. It may have been the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were the circumstances that you were asked to do some translation work in his office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: No. This was not in his office. This translation work had to be done for some people who were then in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the club of deputies of the SDS. I knew some people who were already members of the SDS, either as executive members or delegates who had already been appointed to the government, and that is how I arrived at meeting Mr. Krajisnik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you at some point then end up in 1991 doing some translation work in Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For what sort of period?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: This could have been the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please wait for the end of the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was in autumn 1991 and winter 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that even the live channel does not give the remarks by the interpreters. Since you do understand the question directly in English, Mrs. Cenic, may I ask you to wait for a while before answering it so that the interpreters can finish their interpretation first and then you continue? Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Before you found yourself in Mr. Krajisnik's office, did you have any knowledge or familiarity with his political career or his politics?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Krajisnik was not a familiar figure to me, and not from political life, no. I had heard of him as somebody who worked at the Energo invest company. This company was famous and since I had contacts with the world of business, I heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, we know, and the Trial Chamber has heard evidence, that through the whole period 1991, 1992, onwards, there were a number of negotiations involving the international community in relation to the former Yugoslavia. Did you at some point come to play a part in any of those international negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that the most important were the negotiations regarding the famous Cutileiro's plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was your part in such negotiations and meetings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: As the personal interpreter for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings attended by Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: I believe that there were one or two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall attending -- in your capacity as interpreter -- any meeting attended by Mr. Cyrus Vance?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the building of BiH Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you did attend, you've already alluded to it, a meeting or more than one meeting? Which was it, at which Mr. Cutileiro was present?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Those were negotiations that lasted for one whole day in the Kanak [phoen] residence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that, and I think I can put this date to you, that was on the 18th of March 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that was the date. That was the date when the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was -- was Dr. Karadzic present at all the meetings that you attended at -- with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: At the meeting with Mr. Cutileiro, at that negotiation, he was present. The meeting with Mr. Vance, I don't think that he attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I should make it clear when I asked was Dr. Karadzic present at all the meeting you attended, I am talking of meetings in this particular category of international negotiations. I didn't intend more broadly than that. The -- how would you describe Dr. Karadzic's role and participation in such of those meetings as he attended?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, the head of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that was his official position. Could you perhaps describe the way in which he participated in such meetings?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: At the time, the leaders of the most important political parties and also representatives of every constituent people, in other words parties with the largest number of members, participated in those negotiations, as well as the high officials representing each of the peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, there were the people's concerned were the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Muslims, and Croats, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there anybody, then, who took a clear lead in such discussions on the part of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't speak of anybody who took the lead, because those were negotiating teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you attend -- well, the discussions with Mr. Cutileiro, he was in the chair, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did they consist from time to time of discussions where all the parties were round the table and then also interspersed with those discussions at meetings between Mr. Cutileiro and the Bosnian Serbs separately, then Muslims separately, Croats separately? Was that the pattern?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you also then -- sorry I was too quick, then, I think Mrs. Cenic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for some clarification, Mr. Stewart? Could you tell us were these delegations, you're talking about one day of negotiations or a whole day, is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who were members of the delegations of the different peoples, that is who were in the delegation of the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Muslims, and the Bosnian Croats, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the Bosnian Serbs are concerned, the delegation was composed of Professor Nikola Koljevic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the same question for the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The delegation of the Croatian people, Mate Boban, Iko Stanic, and Vlado Santic. Muslims, i.e., Bosniaks, were represented by Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Muhamed Cengic, and currently I can't think of the name of the third member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any discernible difference in style between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in those Cutileiro discussions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: There was a difference in style. Mr. Karadzic was a bit more short-tempered, a bit more impatient, whereas Mr. Krajisnik had endless patience. He did not leave any stone unturned. He wanted every single written or uttered word to be interpreted for him, word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the third member that you mentioned the Bosnian Serb team, Professor Koljevic, was there a difference in style between him and the others?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic was always a very good analyst. He had a brilliant analytical mind and that was also the case during those negotiations. And he always introduced a new way of thinking into all those analyses and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able to form any impression about the underlying enthusiasm or lack of enthusiasm or resistance to a peaceful conclusion on the part of the Bosnian Serb team?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: There was enthusiasm about that plan. According to everybody's belief, it brought something that could bring stability to the entire state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the optimism was fueled even more by the fact that the Croats and Muslims also had a positive opinion about that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the discussions which you attended, Cutileiro discussions that we've just been talking about, was there talk about a need as a result of Cutileiro plan, for wide-scale population movements in Bosnia to make the plan work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: The move of peoples was never discussed at all. There was more talk about how to deal with the situation, how to solve the problem, how to come up with a solution that would satisfy all the three sides, and also how to implement any such solution, i.e., how much time would it take to come up with constitutional solutions to support any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When the -- now, at this time you were living in Sarajevo, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it may seem an obvious question to you, Mrs. Cenic, but what specifically led you and your family to leave Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, on the 4th of April, my family went for a long weekend, which was nothing out of the ordinary at the time. The only unusual thing about it was the fact that my nephew and my daughter went with my parents because at that time the situation in Sarajevo was already rather unpleasant. However, my family, my parents, thought that it would be just demonstrations like so many times before, and that this would pass. As far as I am concerned, I still managed to visit them and to go back to Sarajevo and to even sleep in my apartment. However, half of the building was already empty, and around my building you could see some troops that I had not seen before, wearing uniforms that I hadn't seen before. When I went to visit my parents, not taking anything from the house with me, fully believing that I would return, that was on the 15th of April, I was no longer able to enter Sarajevo and I was advised not to go and visit my parents because I would never be able to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You mentioned your daughter. Your daughter was born in 1984 so she would have been eight at this time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we still do not know where the parents of the witness lived so I've got no idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We are coming to this, Your Honour, if I may, just a couple of questions about the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, is it right your apartment in Sarajevo ended up right on the demarcation line between Serb-controlled territory and Muslim-controlled territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. The name of the street was Djure Salaja. The number was 30. Today the name of the street is Kemala Kapetanovic street. It is on the banks of the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your parents --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: And between my house and the brings toll hotel there is only the river and the bridge, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your parents were living in Ilijas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: My grandmother, Dragica Borenjic, lived in Ilijas. My parents lived in the same building where I moved into when I returned to Sarajevo. At the time, not even dreaming of a possible war, I tried to build -- buy my own apartment in a neighbourhood called Surakino Selo. However, I lived with my parents because the new apartment had to be redone, had to be refurbished before I could move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anyway, the result was that the whole family in the first half of April, the whole family left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your daughter went to live for a while with your parents, did she?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. It so happened that my grandmother, my mother, my father, my daughter and my nephew all found themselves in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you went to Vogosca on the 15th of April, and you went to live and work in Vogosca from that point onwards, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. Between Vogosca and Ilijas, because I slept in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it that caused you to go there to work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: First of all, at the time, my friend worked -- had worked for Mr. Tintor and I knew Mr. Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's Mr. Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Tintor so I first approached him, especially in view of the fact that I didn't know what would happen to my family that was in Ilijas at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so what was Mr. Tintor doing by way of his work, his daily activity? What was Mr. Tintor doing at the time that you approached him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Jovan Tintor was an activist of the SDS before the war, but in addition to that, he had his own private companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so you were approaching Mr. Tintor to see if he could provide you with paid work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't call it that way. At that time, I didn't know what would happen. I didn't have a clue. I didn't know how long all that would last. A war was the last thing on my mind. I didn't even know what I should ask for. I just happened to be there near Vogosca to be as close as possible to my family, and I was just there waiting to see when all this was -- would pass so that we could all go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But did you then fairly quickly become involved in work in Vogosca, for Mr. Tintor?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: At that time, things happened really quickly. First of all, I helped my family and I also helped his parents, who were old at the time and there was really nobody else to look after them. Also, my grandmother had only two rooms in her apartment at the time and all of them were living there. So I slept on a fold-out chair in a big room in Mr. Tintor's house, which -- in a part of which was not completed. And I was not there alone. There were several of us sharing that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the situation in Vogosca when you arrived on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: The situation was one of confusion. People didn't know what to do. No one knew anything. Some people still went to work, to Vogosca. They stopped going to Sarajevo to work. So that some offices and shops were open, others weren't. It was really a very confusing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was confused, the economic life, the social life, the political organisation? I just wonder if you could try and give the Trial Chamber just a bit more of a picture of what sort of confusion there was in Vogosca at that time.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, whoever I talked to, nobody knew what to do next. That's the first thing. Everybody was waiting for something without knowing what they were actually waiting for. You had to organise your daily life. I don't know what it was like in other households, but people already started asking themselves how long it would all last, because it was a question of survival, how to carry on living, supplying one's basic needs, and I never saw anything that was organised over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put it a different way. What were the changes from ordinary, normal life in a community that had occurred by the time you arrived in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: What I want to say is this, and I think I've already said it: Some shops were open, for instance. I think there was a cafe that was open too, as far as I remember, whereas the others were closed. The municipality building was almost empty and it's located in the centre. It's a landmark. You can see it. There wasn't a lot of movement in town. Nor did people socialise much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- were there any observable signs of either violence or imminent violence?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, anything that you could see, any observable signs, not really. I couldn't observe any. But I think I became conscious that the situation was a serious one. Perhaps I realised this only at the point when some of my relatives or rather Mr. Tintor's relatives disappeared at Zuc. Otherwise they lived there. And he tried to get into contact with them, to find them. So perhaps that was the turning point when I suddenly realised, not only me but others too, that something was afoot. And as I say, you had to organise -- well, there was fear. Everybody was afraid. There was an atmosphere of fear, of tension, in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of Vogosca at that time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: I think that it was half-half, although that's roughly how I would put it because we are speaking about people, human beings, there were Serbs, there were Bosniaks. I think there were fewer Croats perhaps. So you couldn't recognise them as a community. They weren't obvious as a community but I would also like to pledges that most of the households, for instance, around Vogosca, and that surrounding area, that most of the land and the houses were owned by Serbs. That I know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you say half-half, is this -- is it that you're saying that with a relatively small number of Croats, not a very significant number of Croats, it was about 50-50 Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's how it was. But in Vogosca -- well, I didn't know Vogosca before the war very well. I can't give you an exact figure. All I do know for sure is what I've already told you, that most of the households, the houses, and the land, especially arable land, farming land, was owned by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any steps taken -- you described a situation in which the municipality buildings, people were not at work all the time and some of the offices were empty. Did anybody take any steps to improve that situation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: First of all, may I just be allowed to say that most of the offices were empty and when you passed by the municipality building, it was flagrantly obvious that there were no people, and after that I think it was Mr. Jovan Tintor, Mr. Rajko Koprivica, and others, Svetislav Seso Stanic, and a gentleman whose first name I know, and that was Raso, but I can't remember his first and last name, they tried to organise themselves and take over the municipality, if I can put it that way. That is to say, they entered the municipality building. They went inside to try and organise the work that the municipality generally did, the kind of work they did. I wasn't there, I wasn't present when they entered the municipality building, but I knew -- do know that there was done peaceably because there were no people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Whether you say they -- take over the municipality. In the phrase take over the municipality, are you implying any aggression in that step?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: There could not have been any aggression because there was nobody there: It was empty. I don't know that anybody suffered in any way, was killed in any way, or injured or wounded in any way, or that there were any clashes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said that they went inside the building to try and organise the work that the municipality generally did. Did they succeed in that, trying to organise the work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, something was started. Some work was done. However, the municipality and the location of the municipality building itself, that is to say it was in the centre of Vogosca itself, was not secure. It was not a safe place to be. The position of Vogosca itself, its location, along the main road with hills surrounding it, was such that it wasn't a secure place to be. It wasn't safe to be inside the municipality building. And at that time, there was sporadic gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just halt you there a moment, Mrs. Cenic? When you say it wasn't a safe place to be, it wasn't a secure place to be, not safe from what and from whom?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: At that time, nobody controlled -- well, as I said, the hills surrounding Vogosca and Zuc area, I don't remember that any army held that area under its control. And when you look at Vogosca, it's -- it lies as if it were in the palm of your hand, and several people were killed by sniper fire, and they were transported or rather there were casualties from sniper fire and they were transferred, one to Pale and one to a nearby hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How soon after your arrival in Vogosca on the 15th of April did this taking over of the municipality building occur?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: I think that it might have been the end of April, because everything happened very fast. So the end of April and the beginning of May. That's when something began to be established that would resemble law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And between the 15th of April, because you've been very specific about that date, between the 15th of April and the takeover of the municipality building, had there been any outbreak of violence in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: All I remember is, and this date must be checked out, verified, when the attack on the Tas factory took place, I think that there were certain casualties. Some people were killed on that occasion, because there was a bus -- well, I wasn't there myself so I'm saying this on the basis of what eye witnesses had told me, that there was a bus and they tried to enter the Tas factory by bus. Later on it turned out that the Green Berets because of their insignia on the caps, that they were Green Berets, and there were several people killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you've made it clear to the Trial Chamber that you were not an eyewitness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers make a pause between the questions and answer because the technical booth informs us that they are not able to tape the witness's answers in B/C/S if there is this overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's noted. Thank you, Your Honour, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but as the witness also -- if you immediately respond, then the interpreters are still translating Mr. Stewart's words into B/C/S. If you start speaking, then we get on the same channel we get two people speaking at the same time. So may I invite you to wait a while and only then answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was saying, Mrs. Cenic, you've made it clear to the Trial Chamber you weren't an eyewitness to this incident. You had said that you were saying what you say on the basis of what eye witnesses had told you. So you were given information, were you, by people who said they had firsthand witnessed this incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And please could you clarify, who were in the bus that was trying to enter the factory?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: The Green Berets. That is to say members of the Green Berets. And later on, as I say, there were people dead, killed. Caps were found with the insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: They were armed people in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the Green Berets was a Muslim outfit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Green Berets were a Bosniak unit, or a formation of the then-army, the Bosniak army of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were the -- what nationality or what ethnic group were the people who were in occupation of the factory as the bus approached?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Serb, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were both Serbs and Muslims killed or only members of one nationality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, some Serbs were wounded. I don't think anybody was killed, any Serb was killed. But I think there were casualties on the Green Berets' side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the Tas factory was what sort of factory?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: It was a factory where the well known Golf cars were assembled, and I know some Audis were also assembled there, the make of car being Golf and Audi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From what you're saying is it clear that that was sometime in April or is the date rather more doubtful than that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the end of April. I think that's when it happened. But please understand, Your Honours, that all this was happening in a very short period of time because the time I spent in the area was two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that incident at the Tas factory, was that the first outbreak of violence which you learned in Vogosca at that period?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was definitely before the takeover of the municipality building, was it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say when the -- was there then a further outbreak or incident of violence at some point in Vogosca, after that Tas incident?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: The fighting, or rather the shooting during that time, while I was there, took place around Vogosca, never in Vogosca itself, except a certain number of sniper fires, snipers that opened fire towards the centre or at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And without elaborate detail, Mrs. Cenic, at this time, in whose house were you living and in what conditions and circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: At first, as I've already said, I slept on a sort of camp bed. Well, wasn't really a bed, but a make-shift one in a part of Mr. Tintor's house which had been completed, where there was a long room, and where several of us slept in that same room. One next to the other on these camp beds or stretchers, they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And from the period when you arrived in Vogosca, up to the takeover of the municipality building, were you working in Vogosca in the daytime?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: No. I helped his parents mostly. I found transportation to go to my own parents', and I was at hand to help the elderly people in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you begin some form of different work upon or shortly after the takeover of the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I just say that this administrative body moved to the Park hotel in Vogosca, and that's where there were two or three make-shift offices, and that's where I slept, in one of those rooms, not only I myself. There were a number of us who slept at the Park hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll come back to the phrase administrative body in a moment but how long after the takeover of the municipality building did that move to the Park hotel occur?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: I think it was already in May that we were put up at the Park hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the time gap, if you can recall it, between the peaceful takeover of the municipality building, which you described, and the move to the Hotel Park, do you remember how long that was?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I think that was just several days. It was a matter of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you used the phrase, in an answer a few moments ago, you said: Just -- may I just say that this administrative body moved to the Park hotel in Vogosca. What was that body? What was the entity to which you give that label?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, we tried -- well, there were two women, a young girl actually and a woman, or I myself and the girl's name was Branka Cvijetic, and up until the war, she was the -- she was a secretary in Mr. Tintor's private company. And the two of us tried to set up some sort of administration, that is to say to introduce some sort of protocol so that every decision or document or piece of paper should be registered and recorded in the proper manner. That's what we did to begin with. We started doing work like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you were, is this a fair summary, you and Branka, you were establishing some sort of municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to start somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Mostly to Mr. Tintor, because in a way he was the sort of person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall if he had any official position?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Up until the war, he did not have any official position, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there, at any point, a movement out of Vogosca of any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: The Bosniaks began to leave Vogosca, and if I can just describe the situation to you briefly, in view of the fact that I was there fairly frequently, going to Ilijas mostly, there were so-called checkpoints along the way. That means that the road -- you had Bosniak villages on one side of the road, but the road itself was controlled, that is to say Vogosca-Semizovac-Ilijas, that road, you could go that way, you could go along that road, but there was the danger of being shot at by a sniper, and that's what happened to me on one occasion as well. But as I say, there were also checkpoints along the road, both on that road and on the other side of Vogosca, when you go to Kobilja Glava, when you go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was doing the checking at those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Along the road towards Ilijas, the checkpoints were manned by the Serbs. It was the Serbs that were in control of those checkpoints and controlled the road. And you couldn't pass through without documents, without ID papers. But similarly, at that time, the Bosniaks were leaving Vogosca, and, of course, they sought ways and means of leaving. For them to be able to pass through the checkpoints, they had to have a piece of paper, a document, and then we began issuing permits or certificates for them to be able to leave Vogosca without being stopped or so as to avoid any unpleasantness at the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say, "We began issuing permits or certificates," who is "we" in that context?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean Ms. Cvijetic - she was Miss Cvijetic at the time - so the two of us tried to introduce some sort of order into all this because the people would come and see us to obtain these papers. Some of them referred to this as a pass or permit or certificate. They used different names to denote these documents and papers to be issued to them for them to be able to pass through the checkpoints without being stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And under whose authority was -- whether it's a permit or a certificate, doesn't really matter too much perhaps, but under whose authority was such a document issued?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC
utterances.text: It had a stamp of the municipality, a municipality stamp, and signature and was registered in the protocol book with a number. It was given a number. The copy would be stored in the archives and the original would be given to the person asking for the permit. All these terms were used at the time. It's rather strange to be giving things like that, these terms and expressions, but there was the archives and the archives were moved from Vogosca to Pale eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this discrete topic is going to take more than just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You want to move to another one or to stick with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No I will stick with this one but it would take a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, nevertheless, I would like to at least get an answer to your last question, apart from what else -- Mrs. Cenic, Mr. Stewart asked you under whose authority these permit or certificate were given, and you said it had a stamp of the municipality or explained that. Now, was that after the municipality had been peacefully taken over or -- I'm trying to find out what the municipality was at that time. Was that the Serbs who had taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, the so-called Crisis Staff was established, and the crisis Presidency of the municipality, and they continued to manage the municipality, if I can put it that way. So it was under their authority that these permits were issued. The administrative part of the work was done by the two of us, Ms. Cvijetic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honour can see why I was, with respect, suggesting that this really might be an appropriate evening to stop at 7.00 and resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask one question and then we'll stop. Is my understanding then correct that at least at that moment that -- no, let me ask you in a different way. Were the Muslims who were leaving Vogosca, as you said, were they in any way represented in this municipality administration after it was peacefully taken over, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- with respect, Your Honour I wonder if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May be allowed to put my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I also had one point to mention this evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart. The Chamber can ask questions at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, the primary position is that the party calling the witness conducts examination and, Your Honour, I have --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stewart, I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- believe I'm doing exactly that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I put a question to the witness and I'd like to get an answer from the witness. So my question was whether the Muslims who were leaving Vogosca as you told us, were they in any way represented in this new administration of the municipality after it had been peacefully taken over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear you say no and I receive part of the answer in translation, which seemed to start with not as far as I know. Yes, you -- thank for that answer. We'll stop for the day and we'll resume tomorrow morning, not in the afternoon but in the morning, at 9.00 in Courtroom I. We would like to see you back then, and I'd also like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I did mention that Mr. Josse informed me that I he did have a point that he wished to mention. I think he promised Your Honours to read something, as far as I remember, so he's probably reporting back on what he promised to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for another second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honor, may I say myself, I apologise for being testy a moment ago, Your Honour. It's because counsel does try to devise a logical scheme through some of these topics but my apologies if I was rather brusque about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber reserves the right to put questions at the moment the Chamber deems fit and then to receive an answer to those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope my apology is accepted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your apology is accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour the good news is I am contents for the claim to use this document in effect as an index to the Hotic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would invite the Chamber to read all the documents, but the index provided by the Prosecution is of use. It's completely neutral, as far as I can see, and it would be churlish of me to say that you and your fellow judges couldn't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We now get it all back. The Chamber highly appreciates that you assist in making our work as efficient as possible, not to have to make our own -- not to make our own lists of documents. Thank you very much. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of March 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
